record.title: Taste-Bench measures long-horizon decision choices and reports gains from distillation
record.summary: The September 22 preprint introduces Taste-Bench, 502 decision-fork questions mined from software-engineering and AI-research agent trajectories. Models choose between two directions before seeing later outcomes; a question counts correct only when the choice is correct in both candidate orders, making chance accuracy 25%. The authors report GPT-5.6 Sol at 59.7% average accuracy, falling to 21.0% across models when decisive evidence appears only after substantial later work. On held-out engineering questions from unseen tasks, a distilled Qwen3.6-27B student scores 47.9% versus 30.0% for its base model. In a separate 41-task SWE-bench Pro experiment, a fixed executor succeeds on 14.6% with no advice and 33.7% with student advice; correct advice reaches 39.0%. These author-reported findings are not independent reproductions.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors introduce Taste-Bench, a 502-question set of trajectory decision forks from software engineering and AI research, with labels derived from later branch outcomes and a strict two-order accuracy metric whose chance baseline is 25%.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On this benchmark the authors report GPT-5.6 Sol as the best model at 59.7% average strict accuracy; accuracy averaged across models falls from 62.3% for in-prefix evidence to 21.0% when the justification needs more substantial later work.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In a task-disjoint held-out engineering split, the distilled Qwen3.6-27B student reports 47.9% strict accuracy versus 30.0% for the base model. On the same 41 held-out SWE-bench Pro tasks, a fixed executor reports 14.6% success with no advice, 33.7% with student advice and 39.0% with correct advice.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: These paper-reported results do not establish independent replication, broad real-world agent improvement, or transfer beyond the benchmark and the 41-task SWE-bench Pro regime.

evidence_gaps.description: Benchmark construction, model scores, distillation effects and end-to-end advice gains have not been independently reproduced or audited against the released artifact.
The end-to-end advice comparison covers 41 SWE-bench Pro tasks and one executor; transfer across task types, agent scaffolds and repeated trials is unknown.
The benchmark relies on generated forks and judge-model filtering; sensitivity to mining choices, judge selection and domain composition is not established.

brief.importance_rationale: If replicated, an outcome-labeled benchmark that measures an agent’s choice before delayed consequences and a task-disjoint distillation result could change how long-horizon agent judgment is evaluated and trained. The evidence is one paper’s 502-question benchmark and 41-task end-to-end study; it does not establish broad transfer or independently reproduced gains.
limitations: All benchmark, training and end-to-end results are paper-reported; the research desk did not reproduce them.
The 502 questions are mined from available task trajectories and selectively filtered by generator/judge models; they do not represent all agent decisions.
Human review sampled 100 questions; 172 explicit A/B judgments were made, and reviewers could see continuation summaries and outcomes.
Held-out engineering accuracy is from a two-fold task-disjoint split within the source trajectory pool; broad task-distribution transfer is not established.
End-to-end SWE-bench Pro evidence is limited to 41 held-out tasks and one Qwen3.6-27B executor; advice comes from prior trajectories on those tasks.
Exact bootstrap interval endpoints for the student/base contrast and end-to-end comparison were not available in the inspected text extraction; no uncertainty values are asserted here.
Additional reasoning budget did not improve performance only in the tested models and settings.
brief.summary: The September 22 preprint introduces Taste-Bench, 502 decision-fork questions mined from software-engineering and AI-research agent trajectories. Models choose between two directions before seeing later outcomes; a question counts correct only when the choice is correct in both candidate orders, making chance accuracy 25%. The authors report GPT-5.6 Sol at 59.7% average accuracy, falling to 21.0% across models when decisive evidence appears only after substantial later work. technical.claimed_result: 502 benchmark questions; GPT-5.6 Sol 59.7% strict average accuracy; average model accuracy falls from 62.3% to 21.0% from in-prefix to more-work horizons. Held-out student/base accuracy is 47.9%/30.0%. On 41 held-out SWE-bench Pro tasks, no-advice/student-advice/correct-advice executor success is 14.6%/33.7%/39.0%.
technical.demonstrated_result: The inspected full v1 preprint specifies benchmark construction, two-order protocol, human label checks, task-disjoint training and a same-task no-advice comparator. the research desk did not audit the code/data or reproduce the results; numeric outcomes remain author-reported.
technical.mechanism: Trajectory-derived decision forks; two-order evaluation; task-disjoint reasoning distillation into Qwen3.6-27B; student advice is inserted into a separate fixed SWE-bench Pro executor.
technical.regime: 502 questions mined from 2,677 SWE-bench Pro agent rollouts and 1,132 runs on 47 AI R&D tasks. The engineering split has 390 questions and two task-disjoint folds. End-to-end comparison uses 41 held-out SWE-bench Pro tasks, with advice available from earlier trajectories. Paper reports a sample of 100 human-reviewed questions, with 170/172 explicit A/B judgments agreeing with labels.
technical.strongest_baseline: Taste-Bench: GPT-5.5 at 59.5% and GPT-5.6 Sol at 59.7% under the strict two-order metric. Held-out transfer: the same frozen Qwen3.6-27B base model at 30.0%. End-to-end: same fixed executor and 41 tasks at 14.6% without advice and 39.0% with oracle/correct advice.

brief.title: Taste-Bench measures long-horizon decision choices and reports gains from distillation
brief.why_it_matters: End-to-end task success does not reveal whether an agent chose a useful direction before delayed consequences appeared. Taste-Bench makes that judgment observable using recorded trajectory forks and reports that additional reasoning did not improve accuracy in the tested settings. Its paired no-advice comparison also bounds an end-to-end improvement from distilled advice on 41 held-out tasks, while synthetic fork mining, small task scope and lack of independent replication limit generalization.
